ai.literal: Women-natured all with eyes common consume; I approach not, O unfaithful one, your chest.
ai.translation: All women feast on your chest with their eyes as if it were public property. I will not embrace it, O unfaithful man!
ai.modern: பெண்கள் எல்லாரும் தங்கள் கண்களால் உனது மார்பினைப் பொதுவாகப் பார்த்து அனுபவிக்கிறார்கள். அதனால் பரத்தனே, நான் உன் மார்பை நெருங்கித் தழுவ மாட்டேன்.
ai.explanation: In this couplet, the wife expresses feigned anger towards her husband by refusing to embrace him. She calls him an unfaithful man and claims that she will not approach his chest. Her playful reasoning is that all women look at his handsome chest with desire, making it a public good rather than her private possession. The word 'uṇpar' (consume) vividly captures how the gaze of other women feels like a physical appropriation, while 'potu' (common) highlights her refusal to share what she feels should be hers alone.

ai.literal: Sulking when we were, he sneezed, knowing that we to him 'live long' would say.
ai.translation: While I was sulking, he sneezed, knowing it would make me break my silence to bless him with 'Long life!'
ai.modern: நான் அவரோடு ஊடல் கொண்டு பேசாமல் இருந்தபோது, நான் அவரை 'நீடு வாழ்க' என்று வாழ்த்துவேன் என்பதை அறிந்து அவர் தும்மினார்.
ai.explanation: In Tamil culture, it is customary to bless someone who sneezes with a wish for a long life. Here, the wife is engaged in a lover's sulk (ஊடி) and refusing to speak. The husband sneezes (தும்மினார்), knowing (அறிந்து) that her natural affection will force her to break her silence to say 'May you live long!' (நீடுவாழ்க). The couplet beautifully captures the playful tactics lovers use to resolve their feigned quarrels.

ai.literal: Branch's flower even if [I] wear, she will be angry, "Another woman to show you wore" saying.
ai.translation: Even if I just wear a flower from a branch, she gets angry, saying, "You wore it to show off to another woman!"
ai.modern: நான் ஒரு மரக்கிளையிலிருந்து பறித்த பூவைச் சூடிக்கொண்டாலும், "வேறொரு பெண்ணுக்குக் காட்டுவதற்காகவே நீங்கள் இதைச் சூடியிருக்கிறீர்கள்" என்று சொல்லி அவள் கோபித்துக்கொள்வாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet captures the playful, exaggerated jealousy of the heroine. The hero remarks that his wife finds a reason to be upset no matter what he does. If he simply plucks a flower from a branch ('கோட்டுப் பூ') and wears it, she immediately suspects his motives. She accuses him of adorning himself ('சூடினீர்') solely to attract the attention of another woman ('ஒருத்தியைக் காட்டிய'). The word 'காயும்' (burns or gets angry) vividly expresses her sudden, fiery reaction to the most innocent of his actions.

ai.literal: Than anyone, we are loving, said I, ah! She sulked, than who, than who, saying.
ai.translation: I said, 'We love each other more than anyone.' She immediately sulked, asking, 'More than who? More than who?'
ai.modern: நான் 'நாம் உலகத்தில் உள்ள எல்லாரையும் விட அதிகமாகக் காதலிக்கிறோம்' என்று சொன்னேன். அதைக் கேட்ட அவள், 'எல்லாரையும் விடவா? வேறு யாரை விட?' என்று கேட்டு ஊடல் கொண்டாள்.
ai.explanation: The speaker tries to express the depth of his affection by saying their love is greater than anyone else's. However, his lover's mind, prone to petty jealousy, catches the word 'anyone'. She twists his innocent comparison into a suspicion that he is thinking of other women, repeatedly asking 'More than who?' to pick a playful fight.

ai.literal: In this birth we will not separate, when I said, eye-full water she took.
ai.translation: When I said, "In this birth we shall not part," her eyes filled with tears.
ai.modern: இப்பிறவியில் நாம் பிரிய மாட்டோம் என்று நான் சொன்னவுடன், அடுத்த பிறவியில் பிரிந்து விடுவோம் என்று எண்ணி அவள் கண்களில் நீர் நிறைந்து விட்டது.
ai.explanation: The husband tries to reassure his wife of his constant love by promising they will never part in this current life. However, the wife's sharp mind catches the limitation in his words. By specifying 'in this birth', she infers that he might leave her in the next birth, causing her eyes to well up with tears. This highlights the extreme sensitivity and subtle overthinking characteristic of lovers' quarrels.

ai.literal: "I remembered," I said; but "Why did you forget?" saying, me she embraced not, she became sulky.
ai.translation: I said, "I remembered you." But she refused to embrace me and began to sulk, asking, "Why did you ever forget me?"
ai.modern: "உன்னை நினைத்தேன்" என்று நான் கூறினேன். ஆனால் அவள், "என்னை ஏன் மறந்தீர்கள்?" என்று கேட்டு, என்னைத் தழுவாமல் ஊடல் கொண்டாள்.
ai.explanation: The speaker attempts to show his affection by telling his lover that he was thinking of her. However, she cleverly catches the logical implication of his words: one can only remember what one has previously forgotten. Using the word 'marantīr' (you forgot), she refuses his embrace and begins to sulk. This illustrates the subtle and playful nature of lovers' quarrels, where even a declaration of love can be twisted into a reason for feigned anger.

ai.literal: She blessed (me) as I sneezed; (then) having retracted (it), she wept saying, "Thinking of who did you sneeze?"
ai.translation: When I sneezed, she blessed me. But then she took it back and wept, asking, "Who were you thinking of when you sneezed?"
ai.modern: நான் தும்மியபோது அவள் என்னை வாழ்த்தினாள். ஆனால் உடனே அந்த வாழ்த்தைத் திரும்பப் பெற்றுக்கொண்டு, "யாரை நினைத்துக்கொண்டு நீங்கள் தும்மினீர்கள்?" என்று கேட்டு அழுதாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet captures a playful lovers' quarrel based on a traditional folk belief. In Tamil culture, a sneeze is often thought to be caused by thinking of a loved one, or by a loved one thinking of you. When the speaker sneezes, his lover instinctively blesses him with good health. However, she quickly becomes jealous, retracts her blessing (indicated by the word 'aḻittu', meaning to destroy or undo), and weeps, asking which other woman he was thinking of to cause the sneeze.

ai.literal: Sneeze when suppressing, she wept, 'Your people thinking, from us are you hiding?' saying.
ai.translation: When I suppressed a sneeze, she wept, saying, "Are you hiding from me that your people are thinking of you?"
ai.modern: நான் தும்மலை அடக்கியபோது, 'உம்முடைய உறவினர் உம்மை நினைப்பதை என்னிடமிருந்து மறைக்கிறீரோ?' என்று கூறி அவள் அழுதாள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet relies on the traditional poetic belief that a sneeze indicates a loved one is thinking of the person sneezing. The hero, knowing his wife will assume another woman is thinking of him, tries to suppress his sneeze to avoid her jealousy. However, she notices him holding it back and bursts into tears anyway. She accuses him of hiding the sneeze because he wants to conceal that 'his people' (a sarcastic reference to other women) are thinking of him. The word 'நுமர்' (your people) perfectly captures her feigned anger, distancing herself from him by suggesting his true affections lie elsewhere.

ai.translation: Even when I try to pacify her, she gets angry, saying, "You must be acting this sweet to other women too!"

ai.explanation: The husband laments the subtle and inescapable nature of his wife's feigned anger. When he tries to comfort and pacify her, instead of calming down, she finds a new reason to be upset. She accuses him of being just as sweet and comforting to other women, turning his very act of affection into a cause for jealousy. Thus, every attempt to end the sulking only fuels it further.

ai.literal: Having thought, having been, even if looked, will be angry of that nature, 'You, who having thought of, you looked?' saying.
ai.translation: Even if I sit and gaze at her with fond memories, her sulking is such that she gets angry, asking, 'Thinking of whom did you look at me?'
ai.modern: நான் அவளது அன்பை நினைத்துக்கொண்டு அவளைப் பார்த்தாலும், 'நீர் வேறு யாரையோ நினைத்துக்கொண்டு என்னைப் பார்த்தீர்' என்று அவள் கோபப்படுவாள்; அவளது ஊடல் அத்தன்மையது.
ai.explanation: The husband describes the extreme sensitivity of his wife's feigned anger (pulavi). Even when he sits quietly and gazes at her, filled with fond memories of their love, she misinterprets his thoughtful look. She immediately gets angry and demands to know which other woman he was thinking about while looking at her. The word 'அனைத்து' (of that nature) highlights how inevitable and delicate her sulking is, finding a reason to quarrel even in his loving gaze.
